name: Magnetic jewelry

card.summary: Bracelets, necklaces and anklets with embedded magnets, worn as accessories that wearers say also support comfort and wellbeing.
card.aka: Magnet bracelets, magnetic bracelets, magnetic necklaces
card.note: Not recommended for people with pacemakers, insulin pumps or other magnetically sensitive devices.

quick.overview:
Magnetic jewelry is ordinary-looking jewelry, usually bracelets, necklaces or anklets, that contains small permanent magnets, typically neodymium or ferrite. It is sold as an accessory that doubles as a wellness product, and wearers use it as a style piece as well as for claimed comfort benefits.

Its link to appearance is mostly the accessory itself and the comfort wearers report, which they say lets them stay active. Systematic reviews of magnet therapy for pain, including a 2008 review by Pittler and 2012 reviews on arthritis, have found the evidence inconclusive.
quick.how: Wearers put the jewelry on like any bracelet or necklace and keep it on through the day. Products are marketed as fashion pieces, often in steel, copper-toned or titanium finishes, and some are sold alongside magnetic insoles, straps and patches.
quick.risks: The devices are generally considered safe in themselves. Commonly cited concerns are cost and delaying diagnosis or treatment of a real condition, and guidance advises people with pacemakers, insulin pumps or similar devices to avoid them. In the US the FDA prohibits marketing magnet products with medical claims.

lead: Magnetic jewelry is jewelry, most often bracelets and necklaces, with permanent magnets built in, usually neodymium or ferrite types.[1] It sits within the broader practice of magnet therapy, in which magnets are placed on the body to produce weak static fields.[1]

People wear it both as an accessory and for the comfort and wellbeing benefits that sellers and wearers attribute to it. The common suggestion is that the magnets improve blood flow, along with claims about pain relief and energy balance.[1] Within appearance culture it functions mainly as a style item, and wearers who report feeling better say it helps them keep up activity and presentation.

Research has looked at static magnets for pain. A 1991 study of static fields up to 1 tesla found no effect on local blood flow, and systematic reviews in 2008 and 2012 judged the evidence on pain inconclusive.[1] Patents for therapeutic magnetic jewelry have been filed since at least the early 2000s.[2][3]

angle.text: The jewelry itself works as a visible accessory. Wearers also report that it eases aches, which they say lets them stay active, and research on pain has been inconclusive.

infobox: Medical claims prohibited in marketing (FDA guidance, 2000)[1]

paras: Magnetic jewelry includes bracelets, necklaces, anklets, rings and similar pieces with small magnets inside. Related magnetic products include insoles, straps for the wrist, knee and back, mattresses and patches.[1]
Patent filings describe modular links held together by magnetic attraction and combined jewelry and key-chain designs intended for both ornamental and therapeutic use.[3][4]

Proponents say that weak magnetic fields improve circulation, relieve pain and restore an energy balance.[1] Some also make claims about longevity and cancer, which the research literature does not support.[1]
Physicists and reviewers note that the fields from such magnets are weak and fall off quickly with distance, so they are not expected to affect blood or tissue.[1]

A 1991 study of human exposure to static fields up to 1 tesla found no effect on local blood flow.[1] A 2008 systematic review by Pittler concluded there was insufficient evidence to say whether magnets relieve pain, and 2012 reviews by Macfarlane and colleagues on osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis found the data inconclusive and raised concerns about small samples and poor blinding.[1] A 2006 BMJ editorial by Finegold and Flamm noted that incomplete blinding tends to exaggerate small effects.[1]

The devices are generally regarded as safe in themselves, with the main concerns being cost and delayed treatment. Use is not recommended for people with pacemakers, insulin pumps or other magnetically sensitive devices.[1] The US FDA said in 2000 that its rules prohibit marketing magnet therapy products with medical claims.[1]
